# The What, Why, and How of Git and GitHub {.unnumbered}

<small>Updated: January 26<sup>th</sup>, 2026</small>

#| message: FALSE

Git and GitHub are widely used tools in technical projects. Despite their prevalence, many rote memorize Git commands for straightforward tasks without fully understanding what these tools are, how they differ, and what roles they play in a project. In this section, I will provide an overview of Git and GitHub and explain why it is worthwhile to learn and use them over other available options.

## What exactly are Git and GitHub?

```{=html}
<figure style="float: left; position: relative; padding-right: 30px; margin-top: 0.5em; margin-bottom: 1em;">
  <a href="https://www.atlassian.com/git/tutorials/what-is-version-control"><video loop="true" autoplay="true" controls="false" style="padding-bottom: 10px;" width="400">
  <source src="../Images/Distributive Version Control_Atlasian.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  </video></a>
  
  <figcaption style="text-align: left;">
    Figure from "What is Version Control" by Atlassian.<br>Updated February 23rd, 2020. Accessed October 2025.
  </figcaption>
</figure>
```

There are two types of 
<span class="text-term" 
  data-hover-text="Manage, organize, and track different versions of files. Identify differences between versions and allows reverting to older versions.">
  version control</span>
systems that facilitate project sharing and collaboration: centralized and distributed\ [@atlassian_video]. Git is a 
<span class="text-term" 
  data-hover-text="The project codebase is copied as a mirror to each contributor's local computer. Local changes get synched via patches sent &quot;peer-to-peer&quot; through the server.">
  Distributed Version Control System (DVCS)</span>. 
In a DVCS, a remote 
<span class="text-term" 
  data-hover-text="Servers are computers or systems that provides resources (i.e. data or programs) to other computers, known as clients, over a network.">
  server</span> 
stores the central copy of a project, while complete
<span class="text-term" 
  data-hover-text="An exact copy of a project from a server, including al files, the version history, and branches.">
  mirrors</span>
containing the full change history are distributed to individual contributors who act as 
<span class="text-term" 
  data-hover-text="Servers are computers or systems that provides resources (i.e. data or programs) to other computers, known as clients, over a network.">
  clients</span>\ [@server; @mirroring]. Changes are synchronized in a 
<span class="text-term" 
  data-hover-text="Participants in a network act as both client and server by trading resources and services with one another.">
  peer-to-peer</span>
manner, with contributors committing modifications locally and then sharing them with others through <span class="text-term" 
  data-hover-text="Snippets of code or data used to update existing software.">
  patches</span> 
transmitted via the server. The video clip on the left shows this process in action\ [@dvcs; @anukruti162024; @patch].

<div style="margin-bottom: 1.2em;"></div>

```{=html}
<figure style="float: right; position: relative; margin-left: 1em; margin-top: 0.4em; margin-bottom: 0.5em;">
  <img src="../Images/Git Logo 2Color_downloaded 10.16.2024.png" alt="git Logo" style="margin-bottom: 1em;" width="300">
  </br>
  <img src="../Images/GitHub Logo_downloaded 10.16.2024.png" alt="GitHub Logo" style="margin-bottom: 1em;" width="300">

  <figcaption style="text-align: left;">
    <a href="https://git-scm.com/downloads/logos">git logo</a> and <a href="https://github.com/logos">GitHub logo</a>.</br>Downloaded October 10th, 2024.
  </figcaption>
</figure>
```


Git was first released in 2005 and is the most popular version control system, surpassing both centralized and distributed alternatives\ [@atlassian_video; @git_wiki; @stackoverflow_survey]. However, Git does not come with its own 
<span class="text-term" 
  data-hover-text="An interface that allows users to interact with computers through visual elements like buttons and menus.">
  Graphical User Interface (GUI)</span>
and lacks infrastructure for project sharing and collaboration\ [@gui]. Users must execute Git commands through a 
<span class="text-term" 
  data-hover-text="A texted-base application that directly interacts with the computer’s operating system, manages files, and can run programs. It typically lacks a GUI.">
  Command-Line Interface (CLI)</span>
like Terminal, which uses Bash—a Unix 
<span class="text-term" 
  data-hover-text="A program used by the CLI to mediate communication between the user and computer by interpreting commands and outputs. Examples: Bash, PowerShell, etc.">
  shell</span>—presenting a steep learning curve for those unfamiliar with command-line environments\ [@terminal_shell; @medium_github].

GitHub was launched in 2007 to enhance Git's functionality by providing a centralized, web-based platform for hosting and collaborating on repositories\ [@github_wiki; @medium_github]. It does not offer its own version control paradigm but rather builds upon Git's framework, extending it with collaborative features such as the Fork and pull requests. The platform also enhances project management by providing tools that enable development teams to set milestones, assign responsibilities, and track issues\ [@github_wiki].

Together, Git and GitHub enable robust code-based project management for individual and collaborative efforts. Both are language-agnostic, supporting any programming language, and work with IDEs either through native integration or as external tools\ [@medium_github].

## OK, but why choose them over other options?

ggplot(stackExchange_results, aes(x = VersionControl, y = Values, color = User, fill = User)) +

::: {layout="[[7, 5]]"}
[![Results from the "2022 Developer Survey" by StackOverflow.](`r knitr::fig_chunk('survey', 'png')`){style="display: block; margin-top: -1.5rem; text-align: left;"}](https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2022/#version-control-version-control-system-prof)

Git is by far the most popular version control system among both learners and professionals. According to a 2022 StackOverflow survey, more than 95% of professionals reported using Git in their work, compared to other systems such as Mercurial or SVN\ [@stackoverflow_survey]. Git is widely adopted by coding learners, though version control remains underutilized in this group. About 17% of learners use no version control, compared to just 1% of professionals.
:::

GitHub is a leading platform for hosting free and open-source code, with over 100 million developers and more than 420 million repositories as of 2024\ [@github_wiki; @medium_github].  It surpassed its main competitor, SourceForge, in 2015 to become one of the world's largest source code hosts\ [@wired_github].

GitHub is a highly sought-after resource for maintainers and contributors worldwide, including developers working for companies and nonprofits. The pie chart on the right highlights 20 communities outside the U.S. with the largest user growth in 2022 compared to the previous year. In 2013, most users were based in the U.S., but with the year-over-year growth of users from India observed thus far it is expected that Indian programmers will match the U.S. developer population in 2025\ [@github_global].

# Essential Takeaways

With this introduction, we're ready to start exploring _how_ these tools handle version control and code distribution. While the contextual overview presented thus far is valuable for new or beginner users of Git and GitHub, let's take a step back and review the core principles that you actually need to know before diving into the _how_.

**The Motivations:** In a coding project, it is often advantageous to track changes made at each step. When something goes wrong, version control allows you to easily diagnose which changes caused the bug and revert to older, working versions while you isolate and fix the issue. Think of it like "going back to the last save" in a game. Robustly managing a code-based project is only part of the challenge; you also need to provide means for accessing the work for publishing, reporting, or collaboration.

**The Short and Sweet Descriptions:** Git is a system that allows you to save, manage, and track code version histories, enabling you to revert to previously saved versions when necessary. GitHub builds on the Git framework, offering remote storage, distribution, and collaboration for Git-controlled projects\ [@atlassian_video; @github_wiki]. Some refer to GitHub as more than just a place to distribute code, but as a "social networking site for programmers"\ [@medium_github].

# Unpacking How: Git and GitHub in Action

In the following chapter pages, we'll guide you through installing Git, setting up a GitHub account, and configuring both. The rest of the chapter explores working with Git and GitHub through a realistic example and three common scenarios for managing project codebases, with opportunities to practice using pre-prepared problems.

Before diving in, I want to address a common complaint: many Git and GitHub introductions present commands out of context or as need-to-know information, making it hard to see the big picture. This approach makes grasping the basics challenging and often sends users down rabbit holes trying to piece together a cohesive understanding. It also complicates extending beyond basic usage, as it's unclear how concepts apply to your own work.

To mitigate this confusion, the following section offers high-level key takeaways about _how_ Git and GitHub interact with your project materials and with each other. We can divide this interaction into three main categories:

1. [Version Control on Your Device](#version-control-on-your-device)
2. [Remote Storage and Distribution](#remote-storage-and-distribution)
3. [Safeguarding Information Transfer Processes](#safeguarding-information-transfer-processes)

::: {.callout-note}
## Note on Workshop Scope

This workshop focuses on core commands necessary for all projects rather than covering every method for moving files through version control domains. Additional commands exist that may better suit specific coding needs.
:::

## Version Control on Your Device

As explained above, Git handles version control, while GitHub builds upon Git to add collaboration and code sharing features. _All_ necessary version control functionality for your projects therefore occurs locally on your device.

Projects are typically stored in a directory (a folder) containing all relevant files and code. A Git-initialized project will include a `.git` folder in the 
<span class="text-term" 
  data-hover-text="The top-most directory in a branched hierarchy, containing all other files and directories. Your project’s root directory holds all the relevant files and code used your project.">
  root directory</span>, which contains all of the project's version control history and status. Git interprets the project contents as existing in one of three domains at any given time: the **Working Tree**, **Staged Edits**, and **Committed Edits**\ [@Prajapati2019]. Note that some resources may use slightly different terminology for these domains, though most describe and categorize them similarly. These domains and common transitional commands are demonstrated in the figure below.

<figure style="float: center; position: relative; margin-top: 1.5em; margin-bottom: 1.5em;">
  <img src="../Images/Local Version Control Diagram.png" alt="Local device diagram" style="margin-bottom: 1em;" width="90%">
  <figcaption style="text-align: left; width: 90%; margin: 0 auto;">Local version control diagram, adapted from [_"What is git commit, push, pull, log, aliases, fetch, config & clone"_](https://medium.com/mindorks/what-is-git-commit-push-pull-log-aliases-fetch-config-clone-56bc52a3601c) \ [@Prajapati2019]</figcaption>
</figure>

The **Working Tree** is the area where developers make changes to files in the project. In this domain, Git doesn't actively track changes; instead, changes are recycled back into the same file without recording interim revisions. When you are ready for Git to follow changes, you need to add them to the staged environment with
<span class="code-term" 
  data-hover-text="Prompt Git to track changes made to specified files and transition them from the <strong>Working Tree</strong> to the <strong>Staged Edits</strong> domain. Git compares the added files to any previously saved versions available in the <code>.git</code> directory.">
  git add</span>\ [@Foster2024]. 
  This prompts Git to identify differences between **Staged Edits** and already committed versions that are stored in the `.git` directory. Files can be unstaged and restored to the **Working Tree** with the 
<span class="code-term" 
  data-hover-text="Reverts content in the <strong>Working Tree</strong> or <strong>Staged Edits</strong> to their last committed state. Adding the <code>--staged</code> option will move files from <strong>Staged Edits</strong> back to the <strong>Working Tree</strong>, without overwriting any new changes there.">
  git restore</span>
command\ [@git_restore_reset; @git_restore].
  

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Code Like a Pro

When tracking changes, Git uses a heuristic to compare files in your project directory and determine if a file has changed or is new. This change detection method is not always perfect and may sometimes mistakenly identify significantly altered files as new ones\ [@DuMez2024]. Depending on the Git version, this may occur when renaming or moving a tracked file. Some versions interpret this as both creating a new file (with the new name or location) and deleting the old file\ [@DuMez2024; @Houghton2024]. This can make reviewing the project's version history confusing!

If you see this, it's best practice to track a file rename or move action with the
<span class="code-term" 
  data-hover-text="Moves or renames a specified file, directory, or symlink that is already tracked by Git.">
  git mv</span>
command and to stage the modification for its own commit with an appropriate message\ [@Houghton2024; @git_mv].

```{.bash filename="Command-Line Application"}
# Track moving a file
git mv <source>/filename.txt <destination>/filename.txt
git add <destination>/filename.txt
git commit -m "Move filename.txt from <source> to <destination>."

# Track renaming a file
git mv oldfilename.txt newfilename.txt
git add newfilename.txt
git commit -m "Rename oldfilename.txt to newfilename.txt."
```

:::


Once you have reviewed the detected changes and approve saving them, use
<span class="code-term" 
  data-hover-text="Promote the staged version of specified files to become the latest copy reflected in the <code>.git</code> directory. The <strong>Committed Edits</strong> version is what gets synced to the remote server as a &quot;peer-to-peer&quot; patch.">
  git commit</span>
to promote the staged version to the latest copy in the `.git` directory\ [@Foster2024]. The most recent **Committed Edits** are then available for syncing with the remote GitHub repository through a "peer-to-peer" patch. These core commands are used regardless of whether the file being tracked is new or has prior versions saved in the project `.git` directory.

Use 
<span class="code-term" 
  data-hover-text="Summarizes the state of files in the <strong>Working Tree</strong> and <strong>Staged Edits</strong>, comparing changes to the latest, committed version in the <code>.git</code> directory.">
  git status</span>
to check the current state of your project files in the **Working Tree** and **Staged Edits**. Git will identify untracked files and prompt you to add them for version control. Remember, the local copy of the repository does not continuously monitor the remote repository. Instead, it maintains a copy of the remote repository's contents from the last check\ [@Prajapati2019].


## Remote Storage and Distribution

When using Git to interact with a remote repository on GitHub, there are three core commands: `git clone`, `git push`, and `git pull`. These operations will be covered in greater detail later in this chapter, so don't worry too much about their exact differences right now. The figure below illustrates the subtle distinctions between these commands.

<figure style="float: center; position: relative; margin-top: 1.5em; margin-bottom: 1.5em;">
  <img src="../Images/Remote Storage and Distribution Diagram.png" alt="Remote storage and distribution diagram" style="margin-bottom: 1em;" width="90%">
  <figcaption style="text-align: left; width: 90%; margin: 0 auto;">Diagram showing three ways information is shared between a remote repository and a local one. The diagrams for <code class="inline-code">git merge</code> and <code class="inline-code">git rebase</code> are from Atlassian's <a href="https://www.atlassian.com/git">"Getting Git Right"</a> tutorial\ [@git_merge; @git_rebase].</figcaption>
</figure>

To create a local, mirrored copy of a remote repository on GitHub, use 
<span class="code-term" 
  data-hover-text="Copies an existing repository stored in a remote server to your own device, including all files, history, and branches.">
  git clone</span>. 
  This one-time command downloads and stores a complete copy of a repository on your local device. Note that this does not automatically grant you permission to contribute changes directly to the repository; contributing requires the appropriate credentials\ [@git_clone]. Some more on this in the next section!

<span class="code-term" 
  data-hover-text="Downloads a copy of the specified remote repository's branch and integrates it with the local copy. Combines the actions of <code>git fetch</code> followed by <code>git merge</code> or <code>git rebase</code>.">
  git pull</span>
updates your local copy of the codebase to match the remote repository, a process known as "pulling"\ [@git_pull]. Pulling is not the same as cloning; it's used throughout the project's lifetime to synchronize changes between your local and remote copies. A pull operation consists of two Git commands: `git fetch` and either `git merge` or `git rebase`.

<span class="code-term" 
  data-hover-text="Downloads the remote branch contents into a separate local branch for review before integration. Part of the <code>pull</code> action.">
  git fetch</span> 
brings a copy of the specified remote repository's branch contents into a separate branch, allowing users to inspect the differences before integrating the two\ [@git_fetch]. 
<span class="code-term" 
  data-hover-text="One method to reconcile different committing histories in divergent branches. Creates a new version integrating the head of the two branches in a three-way commit.">
  git merge</span>
and 
<span class="code-term" 
  data-hover-text="An alternative to <code>merge</code>. The branch commit histories are realigned so that the leading one defines the commit parent history of the following branch, thus rebasing its commits.">
  git rebase</span>
are different approaches to reconciling divergent branches and should be chosen based on the coder's skill level and whether the GitHub repository is used for collaboration or only for code distribution\ [@git_merge; @git_pull; @git_rebase]. These concepts will be covered in more depth later, but for now, refer to the right-most part of the above diagram for an indication of how they differ.

<span class="code-term" 
  data-hover-text="Upload your recent <strong>Committed Edits</strong> to a remote repository, synchronizing changes for others to see.">
  git push</span>
uploads your most recent committed edits from the `.git` directory to the remote GitHub repository, where they are evaluated for coalescence with the existing codebase\ [@Foster2024]. The most recently committed copy of the codebase is generally referred to as `HEAD`. Git uses `HEAD` in many aliases that refer to current versions—for example, `FETCH_HEAD` refers to the most recent copy of a remote repository branch that was fetched\ [@git_fetch_video].

## Safeguarding Information Transfer Processes

When your local device interacts with GitHub, several security checks are performed to protect your data\ [@about_auth]:

- Verify that you're communicating with the real GitHub, not an impostor site
- Confirm you have the necessary permissions to access specific content
- Encrypt data transfers to safeguard your content from potential intrusions

```{=html}
<figure style="float: center; position: relative; margin-top: 0.5em; margin-bottom: 0.5em;">
  <img src="../Images/SSH and HTTPS Diagram.png" alt="Secure transfer" style="margin-bottom: 1em;" width="90%">
</figure>
```

GitHub supports two authentication and communication protocols: 
<span class="code-term" 
  data-hover-text="Uses a pair of keys—a private key and a public key. Information is encrypted when sent between servers, and only the matching key pair can decrypt it upon receipt.">
  Secure Shell (SSH)</span>
and 
<span class="code-term" 
  data-hover-text="Facilitates secure transmission of information over an encrypted internet connection. Decryption occurs when the correct username and Personal Access Token (PAT) are provided.">
  Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS)</span>\ [@pat; @setup_auth; @ssh_vs_https; @new_ssh]:

- **SSH** uses a pair of keys—a private key and a public key. Information is encrypted when sent between servers, and only the matching key pair can decrypt it upon receipt.
- **HTTPS** facilitates secure transmission of information over an encrypted internet connection. Decryption occurs when the correct username and Personal Access Token (PAT) are provided.

The transfer protocol is defined when first establishing a connection between your local and remote repositories. This is done by specifying the remote repository's URL in the local project's Git configuration and assigning it an alias, usually `origin`. Below are examples of what SSH and HTTPS URLs would look like for repository "ORIGINAL-REPOSITORY" and user ysph-dsde on GitHub.

```{.bash filename="Command-Line Application"}
# SSH
git@github.com:ysph-dsde/ORIGINAL-REPOSITORY.git

# HTTPS
https://github.com/ysph-dsde/ORIGINAL-REPOSITORY.git
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Code Like a Pro

You can set different protocols for different project directories and change the protocol associated with a given project later\ [@ssh_https; @https_ssh]. Additionally, you can define multiple remote repositories for the same project directory, such as copies of the repository in GitHub, GitLab, or other platforms\ [@git_fetch_video]. See the citations for details.
:::

This may be familiar if you've already created or cloned repositories in GitHub, but don't worry if not—the Worked-Through Example and hands-on portion of this workshop will show you exactly where to find and use this URL. For a complete breakdown of SSH and HTTPS with a pros-and-cons table and step-by-step configuration instructions, see [_Transfer Protocols_](../Pages/git-github-setup.html#transfer-protocols) on the Configurations and Credentials page.

# Moving Ahead

With this overview, you have the foundational understanding of Git and GitHub necessary to effectively proceed with the remainder of the workshop. As you go through the remaining pages, we recommend returning to this overview from time to time to better connect the concepts presented here with their application.

            <td class="col1">Patch</td>
            <td>
              Snippets of code or data used to update existing software\ [@patch].
            </td>
        </tr>
        <!-- Row 18 -->
        <tr>
            <td class="col1">Peer-to-peer</td>
            <td>
              Participants in a network act as both client and server by trading resources and services with one another\ [@anukruti162024].
            </td>
        </tr>
        <!-- Row 19 -->
        <tr>
            <td class="col1">Root directory</td>
            <td>
               The top-most directory in a branched hierarchy, containing all other files and directories. Your project's root directory holds all the relevant files and code used your project.
            </td>
        </tr>
        <!-- Row 20 -->
        <tr>
            <td class="col1">Server and Client</td>
            <td>
              Servers are computers or systems that provides resources (i.e. data or programs) to other computers, known as clients, over a network\ [@server].
            </td>
        </tr>
        <!-- Row 21 -->
        <tr>
            <td class="col1">Shell</td>
            <td>
              A program used by the CLI to mediate communication between the user and computer by interpreting commands and outputs. Examples: Bash, PowerShell, etc\ [@terminal_shell].
            </td>
        </tr>
        <!-- Row 22 -->
        <tr>
            <td class="col1">SSH (Secure Shell)</td>
            <td>
                Uses a pair of keys—a private key and a public key. Information is encrypted when sent between servers, and only the matching key pair can decrypt it upon receipt\ [@new_ssh; @setup_auth; @ssh_vs_https; @about_auth].
            </td>
        </tr>
        <!-- Row 23 -->
        <tr>
            <td class="col1">Version Control</td>
            <td>
              Manage, organize, and track different versions of files. Identify differences between versions and allows reverting to older versions\ [@atlassian_video].
            </td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>
</table>
